newsitem.title: USA: Three grandparents of Albright killed in Holocaust.
newsitem.headline: Three grandparents of Albright killed in Holocaust.

text.p: Based on newly available information, Secretary of State Madeleine Albright believes it is "more than likely" her grandparents were Jewish and three of them died in the Holocaust, a spokesman said on Monday.

The Washington Post recently researched Albright's background and reported in Tuesday editions that more than a dozen of her relatives, including three grandparents, were killed as Jewish victims of the Holocaust in Czechoslovakia.
"Based on the information she has received, Secretary Albright believes it is more than likely that these events occurred," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.

But he said Albright, 59, and her family feel the need to follow up on the Post's research and confirm their genealogy themselves. Burns said Albright had believed from an early age that she was Roman Catholic and only now is coming to understand her heritage was Jewish.
He said the issue was "obviously intensely personal for her and her family." Albright's parents died years ago and there was no one to ask about the family history, Burns said.
Albright was 2 years old when her parents left Czechoslovakia in 1939, less than two weeks after the Nazi occupation. The family eventually came to the United States.
The findings, based on research by the newspaper, came as a surprise to Albright, who while raised a Roman Catholic is now an Episcopalian.
Albright told the Post in an interview last week that her father and mother never talked to her or her two siblings about the relatives' fate or their Jewish background.
She said her parents had told her only that the relatives died during the course of the war.

Born Maria Jana Korbel in Prague 59 years ago, Albright has said her political life was moulded by the diplomatic appeasement of Adolf Hitler at Munich and by the experience of bomb shelters in London, where her family fled the Nazi invasion.

She spent the war years with her family in London, attended school in Switzerland at age 10 and acquired the name Madeleine. Her father, a diplomat and academic, got a teaching job in Denver, where she spent most of her adolescence.
Albright told the Post in an interview she found the new information "fairly compelling" but wanted to conduct her own research into her family and its fate.
"Obviously it is a very personal matter for my family and brother and sister and my children," she said.
"The only thing I have to go by is what my mother and father told me, how I was brought up," the paper quoted her as saying.
The information unearthed by the Post is based on documents in German, Czech and Jewish archives, Auschwitz transportation lists, and interviews with friends and family members in Europe.
The Post was researching an article about Albright's family's experiences in Czechoslovakia in the 1930s and 1940s.

Captured Nazi documents now in the possession of Holocaust researchers show that close relatives of Albright's who remained behind in Czechoslovakia during the Second World War, including the grandparents, her uncle and aunt, and a first cousin, died in Nazi concentration camps.
